title: CUDA C++
subtitle: I write CUDA where it earns its place: a cluster-health and vector-search engine for the newest NVIDIA architecture, and a tool-discovery decoder whose reductions are ordered so output bits never depend on the batch.

stats.label: kernels in 13 families, with exact, inverted-file and lattice search
kernel and header files in the analytics engine, tests included
vectors a second for two-means clustering, rewritten without atomics
MiB, the batched decoder's footprint beside the serving model

lede: In the Inference Fabric I needed health statistics for every embedding cluster computed on the GPU next to vector search, over millions of vectors on consumer cards, and no library offered them, so I had the kernels written. Every kernel takes all clusters in one launch. Linear-time statistics run one block per cluster with a grid-stride loop and block reductions. Pairwise statistics run one block per pair of tiles; the dimension loop sits outside the pair loop so every thread reaches every barrier. The centroid kernel shows the style. Its first version accumulated the centroid with atomics and re-read every vector for threshold counts. I had it rebuilt in three passes, and it now scales linearly from 1,000 vectors.
quote: Every kernel has a CPU reference and an equivalence test, so a fast kernel is never the only definition of the answer.
evidence: CUDA kernel development: a cluster-health and vector-search engine of 29 kernels in 13 families, with exact, inverted-file and lattice search, each kernel with a CPU reference and an equivalence test.

CUDA performance optimisation: a centroid kernel rebuilt in three passes without atomics, from 521 ms to 47 ms at 100,000 vectors per cluster, and two-means clustering rewritten to about 500,000 vectors a second.

Deterministic GPU computation: a CUDA decoder with one block per output row, a fixed reduction order and no K-split tiling, so output bits never depend on the batch, in 2,740 MiB beside the serving model.

NVIDIA Blackwell development: decode as a device graph with a device-side conditional, about 518 microseconds removed from every token, and NVFP4 weights 2.53 times smaller than FP8 at about 5 percent slower at batch 1.
author: Corey James
